title: The estimating funnel
blurb: Explain what the estimating funnel shows and why it matters for how estimates are given and revisited.
question: A board member is angry that the cost estimate for a leisure centre has changed three times since the idea was first approved. Which planning concept explains why this is expected, and how should estimates have been presented?

teach.h: Estimates get better as you learn more
teach.body: The estimating funnel represents the increasing level of estimating accuracy achieved as a project moves through its life cycle. Plainly: at the start you know very little, so any estimate is a wide range. As requirements, designs and plans firm up, the range narrows. Drawn as a picture, those ranges form a funnel: wide at the top (concept), narrow at the bottom (deployment).

teach.caption: Widths are illustrative. APM does not fix a percentage for each stage, so treat any ± figures you see as examples only.

teach.body: Uncertainty falls as information arrives. At concept there may be only an idea and a comparison with a past project. By definition there are requirements, a WBS, a schedule and perhaps supplier quotes, so analytical (bottom-up) estimates become possible. During deployment, actual progress and costs replace forecasts. Each step removes guesswork, so the range of possible outcomes shrinks.

teach.h: What moves an estimate down the funnel

steps.label: Actuals
steps.sub: Real progress and costs to date

teach.body: The funnel is a communication and planning tool. It SETS EXPECTATIONS that early estimates are uncertain, so nobody treats a concept figure as a promise. It PROMPTS RE-ESTIMATING at each stage, as better information arrives. And it supports giving estimates as RANGES, with contingency, rather than single figures that imply false precision.

root.label: Estimating funnel
root.sub: accuracy improves through the life cycle

teach.caption: Illustrative figures. Each estimate was honest for what was known at the time; the range simply narrowed as detail arrived.

teach.h: Top of the funnel vs bottom

teach.text: The funnel is about the ACCURACY of estimates improving through the life cycle. It is not a tool for cutting costs, keeping resource use down, or producing comparative estimates. And never quote a fixed APM percentage for a stage: any ± figures are illustrative.

rows.label: Shows estimates becoming more accurate over the life cycle
Justifies revisiting the estimate at each stage
Identifies where the budget can be trimmed
Fixes the final cost at concept stage

items: The estimating funnel shows estimating accuracy increasing through the life cycle.
Wide range at concept, narrowing through definition and deployment as information arrives.
Purpose: set expectations, prompt re-estimating at each stage, present estimates as ranges with contingency.
No official APM percentages: any figures are illustrative.

summary: You can now explain that the estimating funnel represents the increasing accuracy of estimates through the life cycle, and why the range narrows as information arrives. You can use it to set expectations, justify re-estimating at each stage and present estimates as ranges.

A.q: What does the estimating funnel represent?
options: The order in which estimating methods are used
How estimate accuracy improves through the life cycle
How costs are cut back once the budget has been approved
The route supplier estimates take up to the sponsor
A.why: The estimating funnel represents the increasing level of estimating accuracy achieved as the project moves through its life cycle.

whyNot.0: Methods do tend to change over time, but the funnel shows accuracy, not a fixed order of methods.
whyNot.2: The funnel is not a cost-cutting tool; it is about how accurate estimates are.
whyNot.3: It does not describe how estimates are passed to the sponsor.

A.q: At which phase of a linear life cycle would you expect an estimate to have the widest range?
options: Concept
Definition
Deployment
Transition
A.why: At concept the least is known, so estimates carry the most uncertainty: the top, widest part of the funnel.

whyNot.1: By definition, requirements and plans are being built, so the range is already narrowing.
whyNot.2: During deployment, actuals are available and the range is at its tightest.
whyNot.3: By transition the work is largely done, so there is very little left to estimate.

A.q: Why is an early estimate best given as a range rather than a single figure?
options: Sponsors prefer to choose their own figure
Ranges are easier to approve at a gate
Little is known yet, so uncertainty is high
A range removes the need for contingency
A.why: Early on there is little information, so a range honestly reflects the uncertainty that the funnel shows.

whyNot.0: A range is not offered so that the sponsor can pick a convenient number.
whyNot.1: Ease of approval is not the reason; honesty about uncertainty is.
whyNot.3: Ranges and contingency go together; a range does not replace contingency.

B.q: Which of the following best explains why the funnel narrows?
options: Suppliers lower their prices over time
More information becomes available
The sponsor reduces the project scope
Contingency is spent as work proceeds
B.why: As requirements, designs, quotes and actuals become available, uncertainty falls and estimates become more accurate.

whyNot.0: Supplier pricing does not systematically fall; the narrowing is about knowledge, not price.
whyNot.2: Reducing scope changes the estimate itself, not its accuracy.
whyNot.3: Spending contingency is not what makes estimates more accurate.

B.q: Which of the following is NOT a purpose of the estimating funnel?
options: Setting realistic expectations early on
Prompting re-estimates at each stage
Showing where costs can be cut back
Supporting estimates given as ranges
B.why: The funnel is about estimating accuracy. Finding cost savings is not its purpose.

whyNot.0: Setting expectations that early figures are uncertain is a key purpose.
whyNot.1: The funnel justifies re-estimating as better information arrives at each stage.
whyNot.3: Because early estimates are uncertain, the funnel supports presenting them as ranges.

B.q: Complete the statement: according to the estimating funnel, an estimate prepared during deployment should be ____ than one prepared at concept.
options: more accurate
less accurate
less detailed
more optimistic
B.why: Further down the funnel more is known, so estimates are more accurate.

whyNot.1: This reverses the funnel: accuracy increases through the life cycle.
whyNot.2: Later estimates are more detailed, often built bottom-up from the WBS.
whyNot.3: The funnel is about accuracy, not optimism.

C.q: At concept stage, a board member insists the project manager commits to one fixed cost. Based on the estimating funnel, what is the best response?
options: Give one figure and add no contingency
Give a range and re-estimate at each stage
Refuse to estimate until deployment starts
Use the lowest figure to secure approval
C.why: The funnel shows concept estimates are uncertain, so the PM should give a range, explain why, and refine it at each stage.

whyNot.0: A single figure with no contingency implies false precision at the most uncertain point.
whyNot.2: Early estimates are still needed for the business case; the answer is to give a range, not to refuse.
whyNot.3: Choosing the lowest figure misleads decision-makers and sets the project up to overrun.

C.q:
Which TWO statements about the estimating funnel are correct?
1) Early estimates carry the most uncertainty
2) APM sets fixed percentage ranges for each phase
3) Estimates should be revisited as the project progresses
4) The funnel is used to minimise the project budget
options: 1 and 2
2 and 4
3 and 4
1 and 3
C.why: Early estimates are the least certain (1), and the funnel prompts estimates to be revisited as more is known (3).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is wrong: any percentages shown on a funnel are illustrative, not fixed by APM.
whyNot.1: Both are wrong: there are no fixed APM percentages, and the funnel is not a budget-cutting tool.
whyNot.2: Statement 4 is wrong: the funnel is about accuracy, not minimising the budget.

C.q: A team has just completed its WBS and received supplier quotes. Compared with its concept estimate, where does its estimate now sit on the funnel?
options: At the same point, as scope is unchanged
Higher up, with a wider range
Lower down, with a narrower range
Outside the funnel, as quotes are fixed
C.why: A WBS and real quotes add information, so the estimate moves down the funnel and its range narrows.

whyNot.0: Position on the funnel reflects how much is known, which has increased even if scope is unchanged.
whyNot.1: More information narrows the range; it does not widen it.
whyNot.3: Quotes still carry some uncertainty and sit within the funnel, near the narrow end.

reteach.title: Budgeting for a wedding
reteach.question: A couple has just got engaged. How confident can they be about the wedding's cost today, compared with a month before the big day?

blocks.body: On the day they get engaged, the couple can only say 'somewhere between £10k and £30k': no venue, no date, no guest list. Once the venue and date are booked and the guest list is agreed, the range tightens. When the caterer, photographer and florist have sent quotes, they know the cost within a few hundred pounds. Nothing went wrong: they simply learned more.

blocks.caption: Illustrative figures: the shape is what matters.

blocks.text: If the couple had promised the parents a single figure on day one, every later change would look like a failure. Giving a range early, and refining it, is exactly what the estimating funnel teaches.

explain.body: The estimating funnel shows the range of an estimate at each point in the life cycle. Its width stands for uncertainty: wide at concept, narrowing through definition to deployment as accuracy increases.

test.q: In the estimating funnel, what does the width at any point represent?
options: The size of the project team needed
The range of uncertainty in the estimate
The amount of budget already spent
The number of work packages still remaining
test.why: The funnel's width shows how wide the estimate's range is, which reflects how uncertain it is at that point.

whyNot.0: Team size is not shown on the funnel.
whyNot.2: Spend to date is a progress measure, not what the funnel shows.
whyNot.3: The funnel does not count work packages.

explain.body: Each stage adds information: defined requirements, a WBS, designs, supplier quotes and then actual costs. More information means less guesswork, so the estimate moves down the funnel.

test.q: Which event would most help an estimate move down the funnel?
options: Completing a detailed WBS
Adding more contingency
Repeating the analogous estimate
Raising the approved budget
test.why: A detailed WBS adds information about all the work, which allows a more accurate, bottom-up estimate.

whyNot.1: Contingency covers uncertainty; it does not reduce it.
whyNot.2: Repeating the same high-level comparison adds no new information.
whyNot.3: Raising the budget changes the money available, not the accuracy of the estimate.

explain.body: Because early estimates are uncertain, they should be presented as ranges with the reasons explained. This stops a concept figure being treated as a promise and keeps stakeholders' trust when the estimate is refined.

explain.h: Two ways to report a concept estimate

test.q: How should a project manager present a concept-stage estimate to the sponsor?
options: As a single fixed figure for approval
As the lowest figure it could possibly cost
As a parametric figure with no range
As a range, with its uncertainty explained
test.why: At concept the estimate sits at the wide top of the funnel, so it should be given as a range with the uncertainty explained.

whyNot.0: A single fixed figure implies precision that does not exist at concept.
whyNot.1: Quoting only the lowest figure misleads the sponsor and invites overruns.
whyNot.2: Whatever method is used, an early estimate should still be shown as a range.

explain.body: The funnel justifies revisiting estimates at each stage and decision gate. New information legitimately changes the estimate, and the refined figure helps the sponsor decide whether the business case still stands.

test.q: Why does the estimating funnel encourage re-estimating at each stage gate?
options: Estimates must be cut at every gate
Every gate requires a brand-new estimating method
Re-estimating replaces change control
New information allows a better estimate
test.why: By each gate more is known, so the estimate can be refined and becomes more accurate.

whyNot.0: Gates are not about cutting estimates; they are about making decisions on better information.
whyNot.1: There is no rule that each gate needs a different method.
whyNot.2: Re-estimating improves accuracy; changes to the approved baseline still go through change control.
